content: Bowen's disease (BD) is a neoplastic skin condition that is classified as either an early stage or an intraepidermal form of squamous cell carcinoma. It was first described in 1912 by Dr. John T. Bowen, after whom the disease is named. The causes of Bowen's disease include prolonged solar damage, exposure to arsenic, immunosuppression (such as in individuals with AIDS), viral infections like human papillomavirus (HPV), and chronic skin injuries or dermatoses. Clinically, Bowen's disease typically manifests as a slowly enlarging, well-demarcated erythematous plaque with an irregular border. The surface of the lesion often exhibits crusting or scaling. While it can occur at any age in adults, it is rare in individuals under 30 years old and is most commonly seen in patients over the age of 60. The disease predominantly affects women, accounting for 70-85% of cases. Approximately 60-85% of patients present with lesions on the lower legs, particularly in areas of skin that have been exposed to the sun either currently or in the past. Lesions may appear anywhere on the skin or mucosal surfaces, but involvement of the palms or soles is uncommon. The condition is characterized by a persistent, progressive, non-elevated red scaly or crusted plaque, which represents an intradermal carcinoma with malignant potential. Microscopically, atypical squamous cells proliferate throughout the full thickness of the epidermis. The most frequently identified cause of Bowen's disease is exposure to trivalent arsenic compounds. Effective treatment options often include freezing (cryotherapy), cauterization, or diathermy coagulation. Bowen's disease must be differentiated from other conditions that cause papulosquamous or erythrosquamous rashes. Histologically, Bowen's disease is equivalent to squamous cell carcinoma in situ. The tumor is confined entirely to the epidermis and does not invade the dermis. Under the microscope, the cells in Bowen's disease appear highly atypical and, in many cases, look more abnormal than the cells of invasive squamous cell carcinomas. The degree of cellular atypia observed microscopically provides insight into the potential behavior of the cells should they invade other parts of the body. Treatment options for Bowen's disease include photodynamic therapy (PDT), cryotherapy (freezing), or local chemotherapy with agents such as 5-fluorouracil. These methods are sometimes preferred by clinicians over surgical excision. Since the cells in Bowen's disease have not invaded the dermis, the prognosis is significantly better compared to invasive squamous cell carcinoma.
